name: Oak Ridge National Laboratory

profile.address: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Third Street, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Roane County, East Tennessee, Tennessee
profile.reading: This facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Roane County, Tennessee, houses Frontier, a supercomputer operated by the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility on behalf of the United States Department of Energy. Oak Ridge National Laboratory is a Department of Energy national laboratory administered by UT-Battelle LLC, a partnership between the University of Tennessee and Battelle Memorial Institute, and its Leadership Computing Facility has hosted a succession of the world's fastest research computers since the 1990s, including the Intel Paragon in 1995, Jaguar in the mid to late 2000s, Titan starting in 2012, and Summit starting in 2018, each generation extending the laboratory's role at the leading edge of scientific supercomputing. Frontier, delivered in 2021 and opened for early science operations in 2022, is described by the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility as the world's first exascale system, meaning it is capable of executing more than one quintillion calculations per second, a threshold no publicly acknowledged computer had reliably sustained before it. The system is built on the HPE Cray EX architecture and uses the Slingshot interconnect for node to node communication, with 3rd Generation AMD EPYC CPUs paired with AMD Instinct MI250X GPUs, four accelerators to a node, spread across 74 cabinets on the machine room floor. Its storage subsystem was designed to deliver two to four times the performance and capacity of Summit's prior generation input output system, supporting the enormous datasets that exascale simulations generate. Frontier's peak theoretical performance is stated by the facility as 1.6 exaflops, and the machine has been used for research spanning fusion energy science, materials science, combustion and engine design, cosmology, nuclear reactor modeling and biological research, the kind of large scale physics based simulation and data analysis work that motivated the Department of Energy's decade long exascale computing push. As a federally funded national laboratory facility, Frontier's purpose is scientific and national research rather than commercial, and its capabilities are measured in supercomputing benchmarks such as floating point operations per second rather than the power capacity or square footage figures used to describe commercial colocation data centers. When Frontier was announced in May 2022, it topped the twice yearly TOP500 ranking of the world's fastest publicly benchmarked supercomputers, a list Oak Ridge machines have led before, with Jaguar and Titan each having held the number one position in earlier years, underscoring the laboratory's long running position at the front of open scientific supercomputing rather than a one time achievement.

reading: Oak Ridge National Laboratory operates the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, a US Department of Energy national laboratory computing center in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, managed by UT-Battelle. The facility's flagship system, Frontier, debuted in 2022 as the world's first exascale supercomputer, sustaining more than one exaflop of computing performance and built in partnership with HPE's Cray supercomputing division. Frontier and the broader OLCF support open science research for the Department of Energy across fields including climate modeling, materials science, and nuclear physics, and the laboratory has continued adapting its supercomputing infrastructure to support artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads as those become increasingly central to scientific computing. As a federal research computing facility rather than a commercial or enterprise data center, Oak Ridge's role in this registry parallels other public-sector high performance computing operators such as the University of Florida's HiPerGator and the Alabama Supercomputer Authority, though at a substantially larger scale as one of the most powerful computing systems in the world.
